market cap: The total price tag of the whole company: share price times number of shares. Big number = big company.
revenue: All the money the company brought in from selling stuff, before paying any costs. Also called 'sales' or 'the top line'.
net income: What's left after every cost is paid. Real profit. Also called 'earnings' or 'the bottom line'. Negative = losing money.
profit margin: Out of every $1 of sales, how many cents are kept as profit. 30% margin = keeps 30 cents per dollar. Higher is better.
EPS: Earnings Per Share. Profit divided by number of shares. Lets you compare profit between companies of different sizes.
P/E ratio: Price-to-Earnings. How many dollars you pay for $1 of yearly profit. 20 = you pay $20 for each $1 of profit. High P/E = people expect big growth (or it's overpriced). No P/E = company isn't profitable yet.
forward P/E: Same as P/E, but using next year's EXPECTED profit instead of last year's actual profit.
revenue growth: How much sales grew compared to the same period a year ago. 50% = sales are 1.5x what they were.
free cash flow: Actual cash left over after running the business and buying equipment. Harder to fake than profit. Companies use it to pay debt, buy back shares, or pay dividends.
debt to equity: How much the company borrowed compared to what shareholders own. Over 1.0 means more borrowed money than owner money — riskier if sales drop.
52-week high/low: The highest and lowest price in the past year. Shows how wild the ride has been.
beta: How jumpy the stock is compared to the whole market. 1.0 = moves with the market. 2.0 = moves twice as much, up AND down. Under 1.0 = calmer.
dividend: Cash the company pays shareholders, usually every 3 months. Growth companies often pay none and reinvest instead.
earnings date: The day the company reports its quarterly results. Stocks often jump or drop a lot that day. Options get expensive right before it.
guidance: The company's own forecast for next quarter or year. Often matters MORE than the actual results — a great quarter with weak guidance can tank a stock.
analyst target: What Wall Street analysts think the stock is worth in 12 months. An opinion, not a promise. Analysts are wrong often.
short interest: Percent of shares borrowed by people betting the stock will FALL. High short interest = many people expect a drop (but can also fuel a 'short squeeze' spike).
float: Number of shares actually available to trade publicly (not held by insiders). Small float = price can move hard on little volume.
institutional ownership: Percent of shares held by big funds (pensions, mutual funds, hedge funds). High = the pros like it, but also means they can dump it fast.
insider selling: Executives/directors selling their own shares. Routine when planned in advance (called a 10b5-1 plan). Worth noticing when unplanned and large.
10-K: The company's yearly report filed with the SEC. Long, boring, honest — the risks section tells you what could go wrong, and the customers section tells you who they depend on.
10-Q: The quarterly version of the 10-K. Shorter.
8-K: An urgent filing for big news: CEO leaves, merger, lawsuit, etc. Filed within 4 business days.
DEF 14A (proxy): The yearly filing about leadership: who the executives are, their work history, how much they're paid, and shareholder votes. Best public source for CEO background.
M&A: Mergers and Acquisitions — companies buying or combining with other companies. A CEO with lots of M&A history tends to grow by buying rather than building.
SEC: Securities and Exchange Commission. The U.S. government agency that polices public companies and the stock market.
SEC enforcement action: The SEC formally accusing a person or company of breaking securities rules. Public record. Serious.
options: A contract giving the RIGHT (not obligation) to buy (call) or sell (put) a stock at a set price by a set date. Can go to zero fast. Not a beginner tool.
margin: Borrowing money from your broker to buy more stock. Gains and losses are both bigger, and you can owe more than you put in. Not a beginner tool.
moneyline: Not a stock term — that's sports betting. In stocks the closest idea is simply buying shares and holding them.
sector: The broad industry group a company sits in (Technology, Health Care, Energy...).
supplier / supply chain: The companies that make the parts or provide the services a bigger company needs. If Nvidia sells more chips, its suppliers often sell more too — sometimes the smaller supplier's stock moves more than Nvidia's.
